paras: The hanging of Whit Brown was the reported hanging, in 1881, of a Black man accused of murder by people around Red Bluff, about thirty miles below Little Rock. First rumored as a lynching, it was then described by the Russellville Democrat as a hanging done only to make Brown reveal details of the crime, and his fate was not reported.

On 8 August 1881 Robert Yonley, formerly of Pope county and a brother of Mrs. G. W. Chapman of Russellville, was murdered at Red Bluff and robbed of $250. Three men the paper called "negroes", Whit Brown, Charles Scott and Ben Reynolds, were accused of the crime. Detective Sib Bayse of Little Rock and constable Washmood arrested Brown and Scott at gunpoint, then Reynolds on information obtained from Brown, and the paper reported all three in custody.

In the week before 15 September, a private letter from Woodson to Col. G. W. Chapman reported word that "the citizens around Red Bluff had taken the law into their own hands" and lynched one of the accused men. The paper had seen no confirmation and at first supposed the story a rumor born of "the excited state of feeling over the atrocious crime." Before publication it added that "the hanging was done to make Brown reveal the particulars of the murder" and those involved, and was done only for that purpose. The coverage does not say when or where the hanging took place, who carried it out, how the hangers obtained a prisoner in officers' custody, or whether Brown survived.
No report of arrests of the hangers, an inquest, or a trial appears in the coverage.

The episode is known from a single article in the Russellville Democrat of 15 September 1881, published in the hometown of the murdered man's sister. The paper called the murder "most cruel" and "atrocious," recorded the capture "with pleasure," called the accused "villians" before any trial, and mentioned the hanging only at the end, as a means of gaining information, without comment on its legality.
The Woodson letter called the act a lynching, while the paper's later, unattributed information described a hanging done only to extract information.

reader.title: Hanging of Whit Brown
bases: Citizens around Red Bluff were rumored to have lynched one of three Black men accused of murder, and the paper then reported that Brown was hanged to make him reveal details of the crime (A1, A2).

The only report first relayed a rumor that one man was lynched, then said the hanging was 'only done to obtain this information', which implies but does not state that Brown survived; the hangers are identified only by the rumor's 'citizens around Red Bluff', with no number given (A2).

One article in a single paper, the Russellville Democrat of 15 September 1881, printed in two pieces, is the only report, and its account of the hanging rests on a private letter and later unattributed information (A1, A2).
